rows.question: I rent in San Francisco. When can my landlord end my tenancy? Answer as of 2026-10-01.
rows.answer:
As of 2026-10-01, a San Francisco landlord generally needs a "just cause" reason to end your tenancy. I only have citywide rules here, not your specific building.

**San Francisco rule (Rent Ordinance § 37.9(a), in force)**
> "In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction."

The listed reasons include:
- nonpayment or habitual late payment
- substantial breach of the lease
- nuisance
- illegal use of the unit
- refusing the landlord lawful access
- specified owner or family move-in
- sale after an approved condo conversion
- demolition or rehabilitation
- Ellis Act withdrawal from the rental market
- lead remediation
- specified development or temporary-tenancy circumstances

The rule also says "the mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not constitute 'just cause'." So a lease ending or a building sale, by itself, isn't a valid reason.

**State rule (Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2, in force since 2024-04-01)**
> "after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause"

This rule steps back where a stricter local just-cause ordinance covers the building. HomeRule shows San Francisco's rule governing for its sample San Francisco addresses.

rows.question: I'm applying for an apartment in Jersey City. What can the landlord check about me? Answer as of 2026-10-01.
rows.answer:
**What a Jersey City landlord can and can't check about you, as of 2026-10-01**

This is the general picture for Jersey City. You didn't give a specific address, so I don't know the building's type, its number of units, or whether the owner lives there. Several of these rules depend on those facts. Jersey City has no city-level screening rules in HomeRule. These are all New Jersey state rules.

**Criminal records** (Fair Chance in Housing Act, in force since 2022-01-01)
- **No criminal questions before a conditional offer.** The law says: "A housing provider shall not require an applicant to complete any housing application that includes any inquiries regarding an applicant's criminal record prior to the provision of a conditional offer" (N.J. Stat. Ann. § 46:8-55(a)(1)). The statute has narrow exceptions. One is for a methamphetamine-manufacture conviction on the premises of federally assisted housing. The other is for lifetime sex-offender registration.
- **Some records can't be used at all, before or after an offer.** The law says: "A housing provider shall not, either before or after the issuance of a conditional offer, evaluate an applicant based on any of the following types of criminal records: (1) arrests or charges that have not resulted in a criminal conviction; (2) expunged convictions;" (§ 46:8-56(a)). The list continues with pardoned convictions, vacated or legally nullified convictions, juvenile adjudications, and sealed records.
- **Ads can't categorically exclude people with criminal records** (§ 46:8-58(a)). I didn't pull the full text of this one.
- **Exemption:** owner-occupied buildings with no more than four units fall outside the act.

**Drug and alcohol tests** (§ 46:8-60, in force 2022-01-01)
- The law says: "A housing provider shall not require an applicant to submit to a drug or alcohol test, or request the applicant's consent to obtain information from a drug abuse treatment facility."

**Income source** (N.J.S.A. 10:5-12)
- Per the state's Division on Civil Rights brochure, the Law Against Discrimination "prohibits housing discrimination based on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses." For example, a landlord can't deny a lawful Section 8 voucher holder only because of that income source.
- The brochure states exceptions for certain owner-occupied one- and two-family rentals.

**Application fee** (§ 46:8-18.1(a), in force since 2026-05-01)
- The law says a landlord "shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which exceeds $50."
- It doesn't apply to units in one- or two-family dwellings, or to a licensed real estate agent unless the agent is the landlord.

**Unknown:** HomeRule's data doesn't cover standard checks such as credit, income verification, or references. I can't say from this data what the law says about them, so I'm not filling that in from memory.

Many results depend on facts I don't have, mainly the year the building was built and whether the owner lives there. If you give me the SF address, I can check it directly. ## Rent increases
**Boston, MA**
- State law, Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40P, § 4 (in force): "No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind, except that any city or town that accepts this chapter may adopt rent control regulation that provides:"

**San Francisco, CA**

Newly built units with a certificate of occupancy after June 13, 1979 are exempt. Whether the rule covers your unit therefore depends on the building's year built, which is unknown until you have an address.
- State law, Civ. Code § 1947.12 (in force since 2024-04-01, until 2030-01-01): "an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower". It has exemptions, and it yields where a stricter local rule covers the building.

## Eviction
- **Boston:** The city requires a tenant-rights notice when a tenancy is ended (§ 10-11.7, in force since 2020-11-06). State law requires a written 14-day notice to quit for nonpayment (ch. 186, § 11).
- **SF:** City law requires just cause for eviction (§ 37.9(a)). State law does too (Civ. Code § 1946.2, in force 2024-04-01 to 2030-01-01). Some units exempt from rent limits are still covered by the eviction rules. HomeRule has no text for § 1946.2 in its corpus.

## Deposits
- **Boston:** State law limits amounts charged at the start of a tenancy (ch. 186, § 15B).
- **SF:** State law sets a one-month security limit (Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(1), in force 2024-07-01). The city sets a security-deposit interest rate for March 2026–February 2027 (§ 37.6).

## Application fees
- **Boston:** Under ch. 112, § 87DDD½ (in force 2025-08-01), the broker fee is paid by the party that contracted with the broker. Ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b) limits what can be required at the start of a tenancy.
- **SF:** Civ. Code § 1950.6 limits application screening fees. HomeRule notes that no single official 2026 statewide dollar figure is published.

## Screening
- **Boston:** There's a Fair Chance policy that requires individual review of criminal records. It applies only to housing that receives city funding or has income-restricted units. City fair housing regulations and state ch. 151B also apply.
- **SF:** State Gov. Code § 12955 (no discrimination or harassment in housing) is the only rule HomeRule lists. The SF Human Rights Commission's page also covers Fair Chance protections in affordable housing.

## Rent-setting software
- **Boston:** Two state bills (S.2983 and H.5222) are **proposed, not law**.
- **SF:** City law prohibits using algorithmic devices to set rents (§ 37.10C, in force 2024-10-14). State law, Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729(a), prohibits algorithm use in a restraint of trade (in force 2026-01-01).

N.J.S.A. 10:5-12 covers discrimination based on lawful income or rent payment source. | Owner-occupied? Number of units. Building use (for the income-source rule) |
